definition: Overview A class action is a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or "class". Put simply, the device allows courts to manage lawsuits that would otherwise be unmanageable if each class member (individuals who have suffered the same wrong at the hands of the defendant) were required to be joined in the lawsuit as a named plaintiff. See Hansberry v. Lee, 311 U.S. 32, 41, 61 S.Ct. 115, 118 (1940). The outcome of the case applies to all members and prevents them from bringing their own case, except in limited circumstances. Class actions can be brought in federal court under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, (FRCP) Rule 23, or in state courts depending on the basis for the claim. Significance of a Class Action Class actions result in judgments or settlements that bind all class members, even those unaware of the action in many cases. A class action uniquely can bind someone to its outcome without the person ever receiving notice of the action, contrary to the typical requirements of procedural due process. Thus, courts must be particularly careful to ensure that an action can fairly be adjudicated as a class and follow through procedural protections. Doing so can be quite difficult and costly, particularly where the class constitutes hundreds or thousands of members. Class actions do much more than simply address the situation of “too many plaintiffs” to litigate a case manageably: “the justifications that led to the development of the class action include the protection of the defendant from inconsistent obligations, the protection of the interests of absentees, the provision of a convenient and economical means for disposing of similar lawsuits, and the facilitation of the spreading of litigation costs among numerous litigants with similar claims.” See: United States Parole Comm'n v. Geraghty, 445 U.S. 388, 402-03, 100 S.Ct. 1202, 1211-12 (1980). Moreover, “the class action device saves the resources of both the courts and the parties by permitting an issue potentially affecting every [class member] to be litigated in an economical fashion.” General Telephone Co. v. Falcon, 457 U.S.
